chapter: Opening and early New Orleans customs
title: Origin of playing 'The Saints Go Marching In' after funerals
summary: Charles recalls that he and Celestin switched from 'Didn't He Ramble' to 'The Saints' coming out of Girard Street cemetery; interviewers ask about the ramble tune.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Can you tell me, to what extent did the hymn tunes, let us say, like when the saints go marching in appear on the scene, in the jazz scene?
Well, that was on the later run. That must have been, let's say, around 1918. I'm learning, let's say, 1916 and 17. Because Celeste and I, the first one played that.
That's right. When was that? That was around 1916. No, I mean where? I'm sorry. Well, we used to play funeral. You see?

We used to play for all those, in other words, every time they had a funeral like the Swell or the Archfellas and the Pithes, they used to bury it with music then. And so we went and we were playing at the Girard Street Cemetery, you see? And when we were coming out, Celeste and told me, he said, I used to call him the dog, you see, that's what I used to call Celeste. He said, well, Charles, what do you think if we play? I said, the dog, anything you want to play, it's all right with me. I said, look, because we've been playing the ramble, ramble, ramble all the time, he said, let's cut that ramble out. Let's start with the stand. The saint come marching in. And that's the time we start playing the saint come marching in. And the minute we left the cemetery, instead of playing did it ramble, we start playing the sand come marching in. And then when you come to find out, everybody picking up on the saint come marching in.
Well, did he ramble, that was a song.
